newsitem.title: USA: FEC takes first step to consider soft money ban.
newsitem.headline: FEC takes first step to consider soft money ban.

text.p: The Federal Election Commission took an initial step Thursday toward considering President Clinton's request for a ban on large, unregulated political contributions.
FEC spokesman Ian Stirton said the agency's five commissioners voted unanimously to start the process that could lead to a regulation outlawing so-called "soft money."
He said the commissioners voted to publish a notice in the Federal Register that it had received a petition to issue such a regulation.

Clinton submitted the petition earlier this month to try to prod Congress into taking meaningful campaign finance reform and to take some of the heat off of himself from the controversy over the way Democrats raised money for campaigns last year.
Clinton applauded the FEC action, saying it was "an important step in our effort to reform our elections and restore the trust of the American people in their political system."
Stirton stressed that the commissioners had only taken a "pro forma" step required by law.
After the notice is published, the public will have a 30-day comment period to respond. Then the commissioners will decide whether the FEC has the legal power to issue the regulation.
"The commissioners have not decided whether they will take up rulemaking," Stirton said.

Clinton said he believed the FEC has the authority and obligation to take "dramatic action" and urged commissioners to take the next step and begin the process of writing new rules that will ban soft money.

The president, after requesting the FEC action June 5, nonetheless asked big-money donors in the Democratic Party to dig deep into their pockets Wednesday night for the kind of soft money he would ban to help retire the party's $14.4 million debt and prepare for 1998 elections.
"The system has been overwhelmed by a tide of money, raised in amounts and in ways that could not have been contemplated when the system was created two decades ago," Clinton said Thursday.
The White House says it does not expect the FEC to act on the request for the rest of this year.
A regulatory ban on soft money would attack what reform advocates consider one of the prime areas for abuse in the campaign finance system.

Under current rules, wealthy donors, corporations and labour unions can get around federal limits of $1,000 to individual candidates by donating as much money as they want to the Republican or Democratic party.
According to the FEC, Republicans raised $142 million in soft money for the 1996 campaign and Democrats collected $122 million.
The money supposedly is limited to "party-building purposes" but often ends up benefitting individual campaigns, especially through television advertising.
